title: Cartographic Layouts and Leaflet Web Map for EV Site Selection
goal: Present the site selection results through professional map layouts and an interactive web map that effectively communicates the proposed charging station locations.
context:
After completing the spatial analysis in Session 1, this session focuses on presenting the results in a clear and easy-to-understand way. While Session 1 is mainly about processing data and identifying suitable locations, Session 2 is about turning those results into useful visual products. The final datasets will be used to create professional map layouts in QGIS and a simple interactive web map using Leaflet, allowing users to explore the proposed charging station locations.
Compared to Session 1, this session is slightly easier because it involves less spatial analysis and more visualization and presentation. However, it still requires careful map design and attention to detail to ensure that the results are clear and easy to interpret. Using AI in this session is similar to my normal workflow rather than something I am doing only because it is required. AI can help generate basic Leaflet code, suggest improvements to map layouts, solve coding issues, and assist with documentation, allowing me to spend more time improving the final outputs.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes, I was able to create the final interactive map based on the result of the previous session.

Step 1.step_action: Load the final GIS outputs from the analysis phase and prepare them for visualization. Review the attribute tables, apply appropriate symbology, and ensure the layers contain only the required information for maps and web visualization.

nodes.label: Review the exported session-1 GIS outputs
nodes.detail: The participant browses the Desktop project folder in File Explorer, reviewing the GeoPackage and TIFF outputs from the session-1 suitability analysis.

nodes.label: Load the final suitability raster into QGIS and review its default rendering
nodes.detail: The participant opens the Suitability_Map raster in a fresh QGIS project and inspects its default single-color rendering against the Eindhoven candidate cells.

nodes.label: Restyle the suitability raster with a clearer pseudocolor ramp
nodes.detail: Working in the layer's Symbology panel, the participant switches the raster to Singleband pseudocolor rendering and browses QGIS's built-in color ramps to find one that visually communicates low-to-high suitability more clearly than the default styling.

Step 2.step_action: Design static map layouts to communicate the results of the EV charging station suitability analysis. Include essential cartographic elements and ensure that the maps clearly highlight suitable areas and recommended locations.

nodes.label: Build a print layout with a map frame in QGIS's Layout Manager
nodes.detail: The participant opens QGIS's Print Layout Manager, creates a new layout, and inserts a map item showing the styled suitability raster over a background layer.

nodes.label: Add cartographic elements and export the finished layout
nodes.detail: The participant fills in the real title ("Suitability of EV Stations in Eindhoven, Netherlands"), adds a legend and scale bar, and exports the completed layout as a JPEG image file, entirely within QGIS and without AI assistance, matching the workflow document's report that this step used QGIS only.

Step 4.step_action: Create a Leaflet-based web map using the exported GeoJSON layers. Add a basemap, display the suitability results, and configure the visualization of candidate locations and supporting datasets.

nodes.label: Ask for a basemap switcher and page title
nodes.detail: With every dataset converted, the participant asks Claude Code to add a full-page basemap with three basemap options, a title card at the top center reading 'EV Location Suitability', and a view centered on Eindhoven that the user cannot pan far away from.

nodes.label: Ask which three basemaps to offer
nodes.detail: Claude Code reads the Eindhoven AOI bounds and asks which three basemap options the switcher should offer.

nodes.label: Choose the basemap options
nodes.detail: The participant selects 'OSM, Light, Satellite (Recommended)'.

nodes.label: Implement the basemap switcher, title and AOI-centered view
nodes.detail: Claude Code adds OpenStreetMap, Light (CARTO), and Satellite (Esri) basemaps in a layer switcher, the centered title card, and a view centered on the AOI with pan bounds plus a small cushion, then tests the basemap switching and pan restriction in a browser preview.

nodes.label: Check the code and the basemaps in the browser while Claude Code tests
nodes.detail: While Claude Code tests, the participant checks the generated JavaScript and CSS in VSCode, opens the page in the browser to confirm the three basemaps and the pan restriction, and watches Claude Code's own browser tests.

nodes.label: Ask to wire up layer-control checkboxes for every dataset
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude Code to add each converted _map.geojson layer separately with suitable styling (e.g., blue for water, thematic colors for population), add them to the layer control, and use Leaflet's built-in widgets instead of custom code.

nodes.label: Wire up the overlay layers and fix ordering and click-target bugs
nodes.detail: Claude Code adds the five GeoJSON overlays with distinct styling and popups to Leaflet's layer control, notes the large LULC file, and while testing fixes the layer ordering so clicks reach the point layers above the land-use polygons.

nodes.label: Check the code and the browser while Claude Code adds the layers
nodes.detail: While Claude Code works, the participant checks the browser console and the generated code in VSCode, notes the reusable layer-loading function and popups, and looks at the large LULC file Claude Code mentions.

nodes.label: Check the layers and popups on the website
nodes.detail: The participant clicks through the layers in the browser, checking the popups for existing EV stations, water bodies, roads, and land use, and confirms the layer order lets the points be clicked.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: accept the added layers and popups

Step 3.step_action: Export selected GIS layers into web-compatible formats and optimize them for use in Leaflet. Simplify geometries and retain only relevant attributes to improve performance.

nodes.label: Set working rules and request the LULC attribute review and GeoJSON conversion
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude Code to only do the work it is asked and to confirm before making assumptions, re-creates the datasets folder that was deleted, then asks it to read the LULC GeoPackage, review its attributes, and create an LULC_map GeoJSON copy with extra attributes removed, one dataset at a time; meanwhile the participant opens the LULC layer in QGIS to decide what to keep.

nodes.label: Inspect the LULC attribute schema and ask what to keep
nodes.detail: Claude Code reads the LULC GeoPackage (after checking for a Python environment), lists its columns with descriptions, and asks which attributes to keep and whether to reproject from EPSG:28992 to WGS84, noting that geopandas is not installed.

nodes.label: Review the response about inspecting a vector layer's attribute schema and asking what to keep
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude Code's summary of the LULC attributes and its two questions.

nodes.label: Decide which LULC attributes to keep and approve reprojection
nodes.detail: The participant answers: keep the detailed land-use category translated into English, keep the broader category and FID, drop the rest; reproject to WGS84 for this and all future datasets; and install the required packages.

nodes.label: Write and run a Python conversion script for the LULC data
nodes.detail: Claude Code installs geopandas, writes and runs a conversion script that keeps the approved fields, adds English translations of the Dutch categories, reprojects to EPSG:4326, and saves LULC_map.geojson, then reports a summary and flags the file size.

nodes.label: Check the converted LULC GeoJSON in QGIS
nodes.detail: The participant opens the new LULC GeoJSON in QGIS and its attribute table, confirming the translation worked but noting the original Dutch column was kept alongside the English one.

nodes.label: Request water dataset attribute filtering and reprojection
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude Code to do the same for the water dataset: keep only the required attributes and reproject.

nodes.label: Inspect water attributes and ask which fields to retain
nodes.detail: Claude Code reads the water dataset's attributes and suggests three fields to retain, asking for confirmation.

nodes.label: Inspect the existing EV charging stations' attribute table in QGIS
nodes.detail: While Claude Code inspects the water data, the participant opens the existing EV charging stations layer's attribute table in QGIS to decide in advance which fields to keep for the next request.

nodes.label: Review the response about inspecting water attributes and asking which fields to retain
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude Code's suggested water attributes.

nodes.label: Confirm the three attributes to retain
nodes.detail: The participant confirms that only those three attributes should be kept.

nodes.label: Filter and reproject water data to GeoJSON
nodes.detail: Claude Code keeps the three confirmed fields, reprojects the water data to WGS84, and saves it as a GeoJSON.

nodes.label: Request EV charger attribute translation and reprojection
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude Code to keep the address-related fields of the existing EV chargers, translate them to English, and convert and reproject the data.

nodes.label: Inspect EV charger attributes and clarify translation and cleaning decisions
nodes.detail: Claude Code inspects the EV charger attributes and asks for clarification on which fields to translate, whether to keep the ID, and how to handle an empty record.

nodes.label: Review the response about inspecting EV charger attributes and clarifying translation and cleaning decisions
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude Code's clarification questions about the EV charger data.

nodes.label: Confirm EV charger attribute selection and removal of the empty record
nodes.detail: The participant answers: keep the ID column, do not translate the address values but make the column names English, and delete the empty row at index 693.

nodes.label: Clean and convert EV charger data to GeoJSON, then flag an ID type issue
nodes.detail: Claude Code cleans and converts the EV charger data to GeoJSON and flags that the ID column is stored as a float.

nodes.label: Review the response about cleaning and converting EV charger data to GeoJSON
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude Code's conversion summary and the ID data-type flag.

nodes.label: Request correction of the ID data type
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude Code to store the ID as an integer to keep the file smaller.

nodes.label: Convert EV charger IDs from float to integer
nodes.detail: Claude Code converts the EV charger IDs from float to integer and re-saves the GeoJSON.

nodes.label: Request road data conversion with only the feature ID
nodes.detail: After checking which datasets remain, the participant asks Claude Code to convert the roads, keeping only the FID since road attributes will not be displayed.

nodes.label: Inspect and convert road data to WGS84
nodes.detail: Claude Code inspects the road data, keeps only the FID, reprojects it to WGS84, and saves it as a GeoJSON; the participant skims the script it wrote.

nodes.label: Request population data conversion and attribute renaming
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude Code to convert the population data, keeping the FID and only the total population per polygon, renaming the Dutch column to English without translating the integer values.

nodes.label: Inspect and convert population data to GeoJSON using confirmed settings
nodes.detail: Claude Code converts the population data to GeoJSON with the confirmed settings, handling privacy-suppressed sentinel values, and reports that this was the last dataset.

nodes.label: Check the data in QGIS
nodes.detail: The participant loads the converted existing EV, water, road, and population GeoJSONs in QGIS to confirm they are at the correct locations.

Step 5.step_name: Add Interactive Features and Validate Final Deliverables
Step 5.step_action: Add basic user interaction features such as popups, layer controls, and map controls. Review the final layouts and web map to ensure consistency between the GIS analysis results and the final presentation outputs.

nodes.label: Ask to add the suitability raster with an opacity control
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude Code to add the final suitability raster as a togglable overlay with a thematic color ramp and an opacity slider that is only active while the layer is switched on.

nodes.label: Diagnose the raster's broken CRS and ask to confirm EPSG:28992
nodes.detail: Claude Code inspects the suitability raster, finds that its embedded coordinate system is only a name-level tag without projection parameters, infers from its bounds that it is EPSG:28992 (Dutch RD New), and asks the participant to confirm before reprojecting.

nodes.label: Check the raster's CRS in QGIS and confirm
nodes.detail: The participant checks the suitability raster in QGIS and confirms 'Yes, assign EPSG:28992 (Recommended)'.

nodes.label: Reproject the raster and add it with a color ramp and opacity slider
nodes.detail: Claude Code assigns EPSG:28992, reprojects the raster to WGS84, adds it as a 'Suitability' overlay with a thematic color ramp and a bottom-left opacity slider that is only active when the layer is on, tests it in the browser, and asks whether the red-to-green ramp should be flipped.

nodes.label: Check the suitability layer and popups in the browser
nodes.detail: The participant refreshes the page in the browser, turns on the suitability layer with the vector layers, tries the opacity slider and popups, and compares it with the static map; Claude Code's ramp question is left unanswered.

nodes.label: Check the final code and folder structure
nodes.detail: The participant looks through the final code in VSCode, the original analysis in QGIS, and the project folder in File Explorer, noting the leftover scripts and datasets they would delete before publishing.
